## III. Washington (1850–1854)

Mount Vernon Street had the merit of leaving the boy-mind supple, free to turn with the world, and if one learned next to nothing, the little one did learn needed not to be unlearned. The surface was ready to take any form that education should cut into it, though Boston, with singular foresight, rejected the old designs. Boston belonged to neither aristocratic nor industrial nor social society, and offered no standard that could help outside. Women counted for little as models. From them the boy got the domestic virtues and nothing else. The garden of Eden was hardly more primitive.

To balance this virtue, the Puritan city had always hidden a darker side. Blackguard Boston was only too educational. One of the commonest boy-games of winter was a battle on Boston Common—the Latin School against all comers—which began in daylight and generally ended at dark with the Latin School dwindling and disappearing as the roughs and blackguards grew strong. One afternoon the fight had been long and exhausting. The boy Henry, following his bigger brother Charles, had taken part, and felt his courage much depressed by seeing Henry Higginson—"Bully Hig"—struck by a stone over the eye and led off bleeding. As night came on, the Latin School was forced back to the Beacon Street Mall, where a dark mass below, led by a grisly terror called Conky Daniels with a club and a hideous reputation, prepared to finish them. Henry wanted to run, but his brother was too big to run away, so they stood still and waited immolation. The terrible Conky Daniels swaggered up, stopped to swear at Marvin, and then swept on chasing the flyers, leaving untouched the few boys who had stood their ground. The obvious moral taught that blackguards were not so black as they were painted; but ten years afterwards, when these same boys were fighting on all the battle-fields of Virginia and Maryland, Henry wondered whether their education on Boston Common had taught Savage and Marvin how to die.

The idea of violence was familiar to anti-slavery leaders as well. Henry never happened to be actually caught in a mob, but he was sure to be on hand wherever one was expected. The execution of the Fugitive Slave Law in Boston—the sight of Court Square packed with bayonets, his own friends obliged to line the streets under arms to return a negro to slavery—wrought frenzy in the brain of a fifteen-year-old, eighteenth-century boy from Quincy who wanted to miss no reasonable chance of mischief.

In May 1850 his father took him to Washington, meaning it as education, and as education it served—fixing in memory the stage of a boy's thought at twelve. What struck him most, to remain fresh all his lifetime, was the sudden change that came over the world on entering a slave State. Maryland was raggedness of a new kind. The railway rambled through unfenced fields and woods, among a haphazard variety of pigs, cows, and negro babies, who might all have used the cabins for styes, but who never showed a sign of care.

Coming down in the early morning from his bedroom in his grandmother's house on F Street, he ventured outside into air reeking with the odor of catalpa trees, and found himself on an earth-road with wheel-tracks meandering from the Treasury hard by toward the marble columns of the Post Office and Patent Office, which faced each other in the distance like white Greek temples in the abandoned gravel-pits of a deserted Syrian city. Here and there low wooden houses were scattered along the streets, as in other Southern villages; but he was chiefly drawn by an unfinished square marble shaft half a mile below, and walked down to inspect it before breakfast.

The boy could not have told his aunt what interested him; he was nowhere near an understanding of himself. **Slavery struck him in the face; it was a nightmare; a horror; a crime;** the sum of all wickedness! Contact made it only more repulsive. He wanted to escape, like the negroes, to free soil. And yet the picture had another side. The May sunshine and shadow had something to do with it; the thickness of foliage and the heavy smells had more; the brooding indolence of a warm climate and a negro population hung in the atmosphere heavier than the catalpas. The want of barriers, of pavements, of forms; the looseness, the laziness; the indolent Southern drawl; the freedom, openness, swagger of nature and man—all this soothed his Johnson blood. The softness of his gentle old grandmother as she lay in bed and chatted with him did not come from Boston. Though Washington belonged to a different world from Boston, he was not sure he enjoyed the Boston world most.

His father took him to the Capitol, then freely open to visitors. The old Senate Chamber resembled a pleasant political club. Clay and Webster and Calhoun were there still. Senators were a species; they all wore an air, as they wore a blue dress coat or brass buttons; they were Roman. Southern pomposity, when not arrogant, was genial and sympathetic, almost quaint in its simple-mindedness—quite different from the Websterian pomposity of the North. The boy felt at ease there, more at home than in Boston State House. This first step in national politics was an easy, careless, genial stride into a fresh world where nothing was finished, but even the weeds grew rank.

The second step led to the White House, where President Taylor received callers as simply as if he were in the paddock with Old Whitey. The third step—and the weightiest—led over a Virginia road to Mount Vernon. To the New England mind, roads, schools, clothes, and a clean face were connected as part of the law of order. Bad roads meant bad morals. The moral of this road was clear: slavery was wicked, and slavery was the cause of its badness—which amounted to social crime. And yet at the end of the road, product of the crime, stood Mount Vernon and **George Washington**.

Luckily boys accept contradictions as readily as their elders do. He had only to repeat what he was told—that **George Washington stood alone**. On that line, the problem of progress was not soluble. George Washington could not be reached on Boston lines. He was a primary, or, if Virginians liked it better, an ultimate relation, like the Pole Star; and amid the endless restless motion of every other visible point in space, he alone remained steady in the mind of Henry Adams to the end. All other points shifted their bearings—John Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Franklin, even John Marshall—but Mount Vernon always remained where it was, with no practicable road to reach it. Charles Francis Adams never preached and was singularly free from cant. He let his son satisfy himself with the simple elementary fact that George Washington stood alone.

Back in Boston, the boy was more political than ever, and his politics took a strong tone of the seventeenth century. Slavery drove the whole Puritan community back on its Puritanism. The slave power took the place of Stuart kings and Roman popes.

In 1851 came his first lesson in practical politics, and a sharp one. The Free Soil managers negotiated a bargain with Massachusetts Democrats, giving the State to the Democrats and a Senate seat to the Free Soilers. Mr. Adams and his friends would have nothing to do with such a coalition—it was in their eyes much like jockeys selling a race. Yet they took the benefit of the sale, for the coalition chose Charles Sumner as its candidate. The boy entered into no casuistry on the matter. His friend was right because his friend, and the boy shared the glory. He had helped to deduce Charles Sumner from the sum of political corruption, just as he could not explain how to deduce George Washington from the sum of all wickedness. On that line, too, education could go no further. Before he was fifteen he had managed to get himself into a state of moral confusion from which he never escaped. As a politician, he was already corrupt, and he never could see how any practical politician could be less corrupt than himself.

Day after day the General Court balloted, and the boy haunted the gallery, following the roll-call. At last, April 24, 1851, he heard the vote announced that gave Sumner the needed number. He ran home as hard as he could and burst into the dining-room where Sumner sat at table with the family. He enjoyed the glory of telling Sumner he was elected; it was probably the proudest moment in the life of either.

The next day he noticed numbers of boys and men in the streets wearing black crepe on their arm. He knew few Free Soil boys in Boston; his acquaintances were what he called pro-slavery; so he tied a bit of white silk ribbon round his own arm to show that his friend Mr. Sumner was not wholly alone. This little piece of bravado passed unnoticed; no one even cuffed his ears; but in later life he was a little puzzled to decide which symbol was the more correct. No one then dreamed of four years' war, but every one dreamed of secession. The symbol for either might well be matter of doubt.

The boy, like a million other American boys, was a politician, and fit as yet to be nothing else. He never thought of himself as a Bostonian; always felt himself somewhere else—perhaps in Washington with its social ease; perhaps in Europe. He watched with vague unrest from the Quincy hills the smoke of the Cunard steamers stretching in a long line to the horizon, as though the steamers were offering to take him away, which was precisely what they were doing.

He finished school, not very brilliantly, but without finding fault with the sum of his knowledge. Only on looking back fifty years later, pondering on the needs of the twentieth century, he wondered whether the boy of 1854 stood nearer to the thought of 1904, or to that of the year 1. In essentials like religion, ethics, philosophy; in history, literature, art; in the concepts of all science, except perhaps mathematics, the American boy of 1854 stood nearer the year 1 than to the year 1900. The education he had received bore little relation to the education he needed. Speaking as an American of 1900, he had as yet no education at all. He knew not even where or how to begin.
